title: Coset
body:
Given $H \le G$ and $a \in G$, the **left coset** is

$$aH = \{ah : h \in H\}$$

and the right coset is $Ha$. A coset is $H$ shifted by $a$: not a [[Subgroup]] unless $a \in H$,
because unless $a \in H$ it does not contain the identity.

## The three facts that matter

1. **Every coset has the same size as $H$.** The map $h \mapsto ah$ is a bijection $H \to aH$,
   injective by cancellation in [[Group]]. Shifting cannot merge or duplicate elements.
2. **Two cosets are either identical or disjoint.** If $x \in aH \cap bH$ then $aH = bH$. There
   is no partial overlap.
3. **The cosets cover $G$**, since $a \in aH$ always.

Put together: **the left cosets of $H$ partition $G$ into blocks of size $|H|$.** That sentence
is the entire content of the section, and [[Lagrange's Theorem]] is one division away from it.

```
G = Z_12,  H = {0, 4, 8}   (the multiples of 4)
    0 + H = {0, 4, 8}
    1 + H = {1, 5, 9}
    2 + H = {2, 6, 10}
    3 + H = {3, 7, 11}
    4 + H = {4, 8, 0}  = 0 + H   again, not a new one
    4 blocks of 3, covering all 12.  Index [G:H] = 4
```

Cosets are the equivalence classes of the relation $a \sim b \iff a^{-1}b \in H$, so this is the
same partition machinery as congruence classes in [[Modular Arithmetic]]. In fact
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ *is* the coset construction applied to $n\mathbb{Z} \le \mathbb{Z}$, which is why
the two look alike; see [[Sets]] for the partition language.

## Index

$[G:H]$, the **index**, is the number of distinct cosets. For finite groups
$[G:H] = |G|/|H|$, and it counts how many copies of $H$ it takes to fill $G$. The
[[Alternating Group]] $A_n \le S_n$ has index 2, the rotations inside a [[Dihedral Group]] have
index 2, and index 2 always means "$H$ and everything else", one of the few cases where the
non-identity coset can be described in words.

## Left versus right, and why anyone cares

In an abelian group $aH = Ha$ and there is nothing to say. In general they differ, and the
subgroups where they happen to agree for every $a$ are the **normal** subgroups. Those are the
ones you can build a quotient group $G/H$ out of, taking the cosets themselves as elements, and
they are exactly the kernels of [[Homomorphism|homomorphisms]]. Every subgroup of index 2 is
normal, which is why the two examples above are so well behaved.
